analysis.one_liner: Bans stock buying by members of Congress and their families, and attaches a national voter photo ID mandate.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 232-198 on July 22, 2026, with almost no Democratic support; the Senate has received it and placed it on its calendar with no vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill does two separate things. First, it bars members of Congress, their spouses, and their dependent children from buying individual stocks while the member serves, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before any of them sells one — so the public can see the trade before it happens. Violations bring a fee and forced sale. Second, it attaches a national requirement that voters show a physical photo ID to vote in federal elections, including for mail ballots. The two provisions were bundled into one bill, so the House had to vote yes or no on both at once.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters who want members of Congress barred from trading individual stocks while in office — the purchase ban and advance-notice requirement are aimed at lawmakers trading on what they learn in Congress, and the public gets to see planned sales before they happen. The photo ID section benefits voters who believe ID checks protect ballot integrity; it requires states to offer free access to scanners or printers so people can copy an existing ID.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters seeking a check on congressional stock trading

how_it_helps.text: Members, spouses, and dependent children can no longer buy individual stocks or stock-like derivatives (options, warrants) while the member serves in Congress [S2] [S3].

Before any family sale of a stock, the member must publicly file notice 7 to 14 days ahead with the House Clerk or Senate Secretary, who must post it online — letting the public see what a lawmaker intends to sell while they still hold it [S2] [S3].
Violations cost the member the greater of $2,000 or 10% of the trade plus any gains, the bought stock must be sold, and the fee cannot be paid with campaign donations or office allowances [S2] [S3].

Section 3 adds a national voter photo ID requirement for federal elections, with states required to provide free access to scanners or printers at government buildings so voters can copy their ID [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their families give up buying individual stocks and must announce sales in advance, facing fees for violations. Voters without an acceptable photo ID face a new federal requirement to get one, vote by provisional ballot and return with ID within 3 days, or sign a narrow affidavit; state and local election offices take on the cost and work of checking ID and providing copying equipment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress; voters without qualifying photo ID

drawbacks.text: The bill does not fully bar congressional families from trading: a spouse or dependent child may still buy and sell stocks if the trades are part of their primary occupation or made as compensation from an employer, and dividend reinvestment is exempt [S2] [S3].

Section 3 requires every in-person voter in federal elections to present a physical photo ID from a limited list (driver's license, state ID, passport, military/VA ID, or tribal ID), and mail ballots to include an ID copy or other attestation; voters without qualifying ID can cast only a provisional ballot and must produce ID within 3 days, or sign an affidavit available only for religious objection to being photographed [S3].

Enforcement is a fee, not a criminal penalty: a violation costs the greater of $2,000 or 10% of the trade plus any gains, and referral to the Justice Department is provided only if a former member resigns or retires without paying [S3].
Requiring public notice 7 to 14 days before a member sells a stock makes those trades predictable; outside traders can see the notice and trade on it before the sale occurs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stock-trading core is a real, if imperfect, check on self-dealing: it stops members from buying individual stocks and forces public advance notice of sales, though the occupational exception leaves spouses with finance jobs a wide opening and enforcement is a fee rather than a crime. The voter photo ID mandate is the heavier half of the package: supporters say it protects ballot integrity, while critics note it adds a document hurdle that falls hardest on voters without a license or passport, with only a 3-day provisional-ballot window or a narrow religious-objection affidavit as a backstop. Because the two are bundled under a closed rule, a member had to vote for both or neither, which is exactly why the floor vote split almost entirely by party.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 232-198 under a closed rule, and the Senate has done nothing but place it on its calendar — no vote is scheduled, and Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Bryan Steil introduced the bill on January 12, 2026, and it was referred to the House Committee on House Administration [S1] [S5].
The committee marked it up within two days and ordered it reported as amended on a 7-4 vote, reporting it to the House on February 3, 2026 [S5].
On July 22, 2026, the House debated the bill under a closed rule (no floor amendments allowed) along with five other measures [S5].

Rep. Magaziner moved to send the bill back to committee (a motion to recommit, a common last-chance tactic to change or delay a bill); it failed 211-218, with all 211 votes for it coming from Democrats and all 218 against from Republicans [S5] [S6].
The bill passed 232-198: all 218 Republicans voting were in favor, 13 of the 211 voting Democrats were in favor, and 198 Democrats and 1 independent were opposed [S7].
The Senate received the bill on July 23, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate calendar on August 6, 2026 (Calendar No. 548); no further action has been taken [S3] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, members of Congress and their families: they can still buy and sell stocks freely while the bill waits on the Senate calendar. Supporters of voter ID laws also gained a House-passed vehicle for a national mandate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress, who can still trade stocks

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their immediate families
industries.note: The bill ends their ability to buy individual stocks and requires public notice before selling, backed by fees. Their existing freedom to trade while holding legislative power is exactly what the bill curtails.

They must check photo ID for every federal-election voter, notify registrants of the rule, and provide free public access to scanners or printers for copying IDs. The federal mandate adds workload and equipment duties with no new funding in the bill.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits on the Senate calendar with no vote scheduled and no Senate sponsor activity in the record. A member-trading restriction passed this way could stall there for the rest of the Congress unless Senate leadership schedules it — a common fate for House-passed ethics measures. The voter ID rider also makes the package harder for Senate Democrats to support, so the more likely paths are inaction or a Senate rewrite that separates the two provisions.
